what: Two free rollers wait on the same fixed incline behind one common gate. Each roller has 39 placed parts and 73.28 g of canonical catalog mass, two identical outer wheels and a centered mass distribution. The fixed incline is 6.842773°. The green roller starts with its paired ballast close to the axis; the orange roller carries the same ballast farther out. Motor A lifts the gate, then holds it clear while gravity and contact move the rollers. Neither roller has a motor, axle bearing to the frame or imposed path. Compare their downhill travel before either touches a spring catch. The supplied comparison exchanges the ballast layouts between the lanes while keeping the green and orange lane colors.
try: In Robot Lab, choose File → Open and import models/rimrun.ldr afresh. Paste the full source of programs/rimrun.bw into the Code tab and choose ⇦ To blocks. Return to Robot Lab and use its Run button, which connects the loaded SPIKE program to the simulated hub. These are source-verified application routes; browser interaction has not been tested for this add-on. The supplied catalog files are a proposal and do not install a gallery entry.

Before running, predict whether equal weight and equal wheel size imply equal downhill motion. Inspect both opposed ballast packages. Color identifies the lane; distance of the ballast from the rolling axis is the quantity being changed.

The program homes motor A to 0° at 60°/s, holds for 1.5 seconds and checks the actual angle. It then requests +100° at 400°/s, holds open for three seconds and returns to 0° at 120°/s under a finite watchdog. These are command targets, not measured trajectories. Watch the actual release from the side. Compare the roller centers crossing the same downhill position, or compare their positions at the same time after release. End the rolling comparison before a wheel touches any spring shoe or backup wall.

Check that translation is accompanied by rolling. A spoke turning without the corresponding travel, or travel without enough turning, indicates slip. For rolling without slip, distance along the track is approximately the rolling radius times the rotation angle in radians. A convincing result needs this check as well as a finishing order.

Let the finite program finish. It holds the gate open, returns the gate to its saved angle and stops. Returning the gate does not restore the rollers' original positions, angular phases or velocities, or the passive catches' original state.

Predict which result should exchange lanes. Use File → Open to import the complete models/rimrun-swapped.ldr scene afresh, then run the same programs/rimrun.bw source. Green now carries the outer ballast and orange the inner ballast. The runway, starting wheel poses, part inventory, total masses and release commands are unchanged.

Compare both runs before spring-shoe or wall contact. Does the earlier arrival follow the inner ballast when it moves to the other lane? Reload the complete saved model before every repeat, including after an interruption. An encoder reset or another Run on the used scene is not a fresh trial.
why: Gravity supplies both translational and rotational kinetic energy during rolling. The total mass sets the available gravitational energy, but it does not say how that energy is divided. Moving the same balanced ballast outward increases the axial moment of inertia while leaving mass, center of mass and outer rolling radius unchanged. For rolling without slip, the outer-ballast configuration therefore needs more rotational energy for a given center speed and has a smaller downhill acceleration. Static friction supplies the torque that starts the rotation; in the ideal no-slip model it does no work at the stationary contact point. If the wheels slip, the simple rolling relation is no longer sufficient.
matters: Mass distribution matters even when a scale and the outside dimensions cannot distinguish two objects. In the fresh native pair, the inner-ballast configuration won in both lanes. The scoped rolling comparison passes all 109 retained original gates per run and all eight original comparison checks apart from the separate whole-run aggregate. Full native qualification remains FAIL: later settling and catch limits are not met. The watchdog diagnostic also fails its final angular-speed limit. These failures remain in their original reports; a successful rolling comparison does not qualify the complete machine. Browser integration, manual control and a physical build are untested.
question: Both rollers contain the same parts and have the same total mass and wheel radius. Which ballast layout should reach a chosen downhill position first, and what should happen when the layouts exchange lanes?
answer: The inner-ballast layout arrived first in both fresh native runs. At 200 mm of travel it arrived 25.930 ms earlier in the main scene and 25.387 ms earlier after the lane exchange. When the inner roller reached that position, the outer roller was still 14.424 mm and 14.141 mm behind, respectively. Bringing mass closer to the axis reduces the axial moment of inertia, so more of the same gravitational energy appears as translation. The observed advantage followed the inner ballast into the other lane, rather than following green or the left lane. These are results for the free-rolling comparison before catch contact; the complete-run verdict remains FAIL.
further: Define kappa = I_cm/(M R²), with I_cm about the roller's central rolling axis. The recorded native values are approximately 0.307316 for inner ballast and 0.409080 for outer ballast. Their ideal acceleration ratio is 1.077842. At the same height drop, the ideal ratio of rotational to translational kinetic energy is kappa. Equal mass therefore does not imply equal speed, and equal wheel radius does not imply equal moment of inertia.

Multiplying every mass by the same factor without changing its position would leave kappa and the ideal rolling acceleration unchanged. Moving the ballast outward is different: it changes I_cm/(M R²). The opposed packages keep the center of mass centered; one unbalanced package would add a different experiment with orientation-dependent gravity torque.

The native solver uses canonical part masses and primitive collision shapes. Contact friction and ordinary damping remain active. Its additional tire rolling-resistance routine requires a coaxial hinge and does not apply to these entirely free rigid rollers. The measurements establish the comparison within this representation; they are not a calibration of real tire losses or a prediction of hardware finish times.

Carry Ratio already explains how rotational inertia affects a ball transported by a moving tray. Switchback Lift sends one ball down ramps, and Travel Dial checks rolling as an odometer. RimRun compares two fixed ballast layouts at matched mass and radius under gravity, then exchanges their lanes. Afterturn and Inertia Loop relocate masses during driven reaction-wheel cycles instead.

The recorded position fits use the unchanged native damping coefficient, 0.05 per second. They give driving accelerations of 0.884448 and 0.815241 m/s² for inner and outer ballast in the main scene, and 0.883437 and 0.817677 m/s² after the lane exchange. The corresponding ratios are 1.084891 and 1.080423, compared with the ideal 1.077842. Across both runs the largest mismatch between traveled distance and rolling arc in the declared interval was 0.005282 mm. These checks support an inertia comparison rather than an interpretation based only on finishing order.

Four independent spring shoes act after the free-rolling measurement region, with a fixed backup wall beyond them. They are passive catches, not finish-line sensors or reset devices. A physical assembly needs four intact spring-equipped 9L shock units; the simulator draws each cylinder and rod and supplies the spring through native parameters, without a separate coil mesh or mass. Full catch qualification fails: the largest transverse slider gap is 0.731458 mm against 0.5 mm, and the backup-wall penetration upper bound reaches 0.946783 mm against 0.35 mm. Final roller-rest limits also fail. Reload the complete scene before every trial.

A separate watchdog test shortened only the deadline from 12 seconds to 0.12 seconds and interrupted a real powered home after 1.6445° of gate motion. The failure flag, absence of late motion commands, finite exit and held-angle range all passed. Its maximum final angular speed was 3.159365°/s against a 2°/s limit, so the watchdog test remains FAIL. This diagnostic is not a physical jam test. The unchanged full reports and scoped result are packaged in evidence/qualification/, including rolling-comparison.json, main-observer.json, swapped-observer.json, pair-observer.json and watchdog/watchdog.json.
formula: Ideal rolling from rest without slip: kappa = I_cm/(M R²); a = g sin(alpha)/(1 + kappa); v² = 2gh/(1 + kappa); K_rot/K_trans = kappa; v = R omega. Alpha is the fixed incline, h the actual center-of-mass height lost, R the rolling radius, and omega the angular speed. These relations predict the effect of inertia; actual poses and velocities must establish the trajectory, release conditions and validity of rolling without slip.
